paper.title: R 2 Flow: Recursive Self-Improvement via Recursive Skill Evolution
paper.abstract:
Abstract LLM-based agents can improve themselves across tasks by reusing and revising the skills they orchestrate into executable procedures. Flow-based training fits this loop: it samples procedures in proportion to reward, and the flow through each skill credits it for the next library revision. Three obstacles stand in the way of making this self-improvement reliable: flow training suffers strategy collapse over tree-structured histories; nonnegative flow-based credit rewards frequent use as if it were benefit; and library edits rest on the task reward the policy optimizes. We introduce R 2 Flow , a recursive self-improvement framework that alternates policy learning, independent verification, and
versioned skill-library updates on a shared-state orchestration graph. The graph
merges histories that differ only in the order of independent steps, allowing
flow training to pool evidence across equivalent executions. A flow-share readout of the trained flow, invariant to the backward policy, and a separate signed utility rank which skills to change, verifier evidence decides
whether an edit is warranted, and a residual-variance plateau sets when to update. Committed edits reshape the graph the next policy learns on, realizing recursive skill evolution. Across question answering, mathematical reasoning,
interactive decision making, and code generation, R 2 Flow improves task
accuracy and library-edit precision over heuristic orchestration, reinforcement
learning, and skill-evolution baselines, and transfers across executors. Code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/r2flow .

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.33867v1 [cs.AI] 27 Sep 2026 R 2 Flow: Recursive Self-Improvement via Recursive Skill Evolution Mingda Zhang Qiang Huang Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen Fudan University Yanjin Li Zijia Wang Qika Lin Affiliation: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign University of Oxford National University of Singapore Xiaoying Tang Tiesunlong Shen Affiliation: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign University of Oxford National University of Singapore Abstract LLM-based agents can improve themselves across tasks by reusing and revising the skills they orchestrate into executable procedures. Flow-based training fits this loop: it samples procedures in proportion to reward, and the flow through each skill credits it for the next library revision. Three obstacles stand in the way of making this self-improvement reliable: flow training suffers strategy collapse over tree-structured histories; nonnegative flow-based credit rewards frequent use as if it were benefit; and library edits rest on the task reward the policy optimizes. We introduce R 2 Flow , a recursive self-improvement framework that alternates policy learning, independent verification, and versioned skill-library updates on a shared-state orchestration graph. The graph merges histories that differ only in the order of independent steps, allowing flow training to pool evidence across equivalent executions. A flow-share readout of the trained flow, invariant to the backward policy, and a separate signed utility rank which skills to change, verifier evidence decides whether an edit is warranted, and a residual-variance plateau sets when to update. Committed edits reshape the graph the next policy learns on, realizing recursive skill evolution. Across question answering, mathematical reasoning, interactive decision making, and code generation, R 2 Flow improves task accuracy and library-edit precision over heuristic orchestration, reinforcement learning, and skill-evolution baselines, and transfers across executors. Code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/r2flow . 1 Introduction Figure 1: R 2 Flow trains a flow on shared states (inner loop), reads share and signed utility separately, and gates library edits on verified evidence (outer loop). In recent years, LLM-based agentic systems have come to orchestrate reusable skills into executable procedures ( Yao et al., 2022b ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) , shifting the unit of automation from a single answer to an entire procedure. A central goal is therefore not only to complete a task but to improve the procedure used later ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . This makes self-improvement a recursive loop: each phase trains the policy on a versioned library and updates that library from what it learned, and the next phase repeats this on the new library. Without human review, such a loop must admit each update on evidence outside the training reward. Task orchestration organizes primitive actions and reusable skills into structured trajectories on an orchestration graph ( Figure 1 , panel 1), where each node is an execution state and each edge is one orchestration event, which makes complex tasks more controllable and composable ( Zhuge et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yun et al., 2026 ; Tieu et al., 2026 ) . Orchestration has accordingly evolved from static human-authored pipelines to graphs generated or edited at run time ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ; Yue et al., 2026 ) , and further to policies trained directly from execution feedback ( Zhang et al., 2026e ; Zhang, 2026b ) . However, these policies are still trained on tree-structured histories, where the same steps taken in a different order are never recognised as one procedure. Figure 2: Four orchestration paradigms. (a) Workflow graph optimization hides a harmful skill in the return. (b) Flow-driven orchestration learns A ​ B AB and B ​ A BA twice on a history tree, so evidence never pools. (c) Posterior-guided evolution scores reliability, not signed utility, so success reads as benefit. (d) R 2 Flow pools evidence on shared states, separates share from utility, and commits verified edits. To address these issues, graph-based orchestration ( Figure 2 a) retrieves prebuilt skills or searches and edits workflow graphs at run time ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhuge et al., 2024 ; Yun et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Tieu et al., 2026 ) . Step-level credit assignment ( Figure 2 b) converts a terminal reward into finer-grained signals through process reward models, hindsight advantage estimation, and GFlowNet balance objectives that sample in proportion to reward ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Malkin et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2026e ; Tao et al., 2026 ; Tan et al., 2026 ) . Dynamic skill libraries ( Figure 2 c) grow capability by curating skills with LLM-as-judge prompting, execution feedback, or posterior beliefs over skill reliability ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2026 ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ) . However, joining these lines of work into one loop faces three challenges. (i) Strategy collapse. When a state is the full interaction history, every state has exactly one parent, so the orchestration graph is a tree and the backward policy is trivially one ( Malkin et al., 2022 ; Fawkes & Hartford, 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Executions that differ only in the order of independent steps sit on different branches and never share evidence; the flow then spreads probability over reorderings of one procedure rather than across genuinely different strategies, so a procedure with more admissible orderings receives proportionally more sampling mass, and more weight in the next library edit ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2026e ) . (ii) Indiscriminate credit assignment. Flow shares and usage counts are non-negative by construction and reliability posteriors score whether a call succeeds, so none says whether a skill helps, and a frequently invoked harmful skill looks critical and survives into the next library ( Zhang et al., 2026e ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Li, 2026 ) . (iii) Unverified skill evolution. Edits are admitted on the same task reward whose attribution is in question, and on point estimates that cannot separate insufficient evidence from confirmed failure, so a skill can be pruned before its evidence accumulates ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026f ; Zhang, 2026c ; Zhang, 2026a ) . We introduce R 2 Flow ( Figure 2 d), running this loop through three designs, each serving the library update. The first, the Orchestration Graph , replaces the history tree of trained orchestration policies: it merges histories differing only in the order of independent steps into one state, so their evidence pools at that state; when a merged state has several legal predecessors, the backward policy is a genuine choice among them. Built on the graph, we further propose flow share : a flow network is trained on the shared states with the balance objective R 2 TB, and each skill’s share of the flow is read from the trained policy’s rollouts weighted by their residuals, a readout invariant to the backward policy. In contrast to credit that reads use as benefit, it is kept separate from a signed utility that says whether the skill helps. R 2 Flow then performs verifier-gated skill-library updates , replacing admission on the task reward: independent verifiers label skill invocations, edge flow picks which ones to verify, and an edit refines or prunes a skill only when verified evidence supports it, waiting otherwise. The R 2 TB residual also times the loop: a plateau in its variance ends a phase and triggers the next library update. Together the designs close one recursive loop: each phase trains on the library the previous phase committed, and its readouts, posterior and residual decide the next commit. We evaluate on twelve datasets across four task domains, six held out, reporting task accuracy, executor transfer, and library-edit precision against heuristic orchestration, reinforcement learning ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) , and skill-evolution baselines ( Ni et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . 2 Related Work Self-Improving Agents. Self-improving agents rewrite scaffolding, meta-agent designs, or their own logic and code ( Zelikman et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) , in loops framed as bounded or open-ended self-modification ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . Skill evolution co-trains the library with the policy ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026e ) , Bayesian curation adds finite-sample uncertainty, and verification screens edits ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Most admit an edit on task-level outcomes, so the edit is judged by the signal whose attribution is in question, where an optimiser exploits its evaluator ( Thaman, 2026 ) . R 2 Flow instead admits library edits on verifier labels outside the reward. Agent Task Orchestration. LLM agents orchestrate tasks in loops that plan, act, and revise on execution feedback ( Yao et al., 2022b ; Yue et al., 2026 ) . Existing work spans operator graphs generated by search or edited under structured feedback ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhuge et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ; Li et al., 2026a ; Tieu et al., 2026 ) , reusable skill memory, and self-evolving architectures ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Tang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026b ; Bai et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . Trained orchestration policies define states over raw histories, so a procedure and its reorderings never share statistics. R 2 Flow instead trains its flow on a dependency-aware shared-state graph of executable histories, where reorderings meet at one state ( Yu et al., 2024 , as in reasoning DAGs;) . 3 Preliminaries Definition 1: Orchestration State Graph. Task orchestration is a directed graph 𝒢 \mathcal{G} whose vertices are interaction histories H t H_{t} and whose edges are orchestration events. The update H t = H t − 1 ⊕ ( r t , e t , o t exec ) H_{t}=H_{t-1}\oplus(r_{t},e_{t},o_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}) appends one record, so 𝒢 \mathcal{G} is acyclic and every non-root history has one parent. Definition 2: Orchestration Trajectory. A complete path from the initial history H 0 H_{0} to a terminal state defines an orchestration trajectory: τ = { ( r t , e t , o t exec ) } t = 1 T ⇒ y q , \tau=\bigl\{(r_{t},\ e_{t},\ o_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}})\bigr\}_{t=1}^{T}\ \Rightarrow\ y_{q}, (1) where r t r_{t} is the reasoning text, e t = ( u t , args t ) e_{t}=(u_{t},\mathrm{args}_{t}) the event, and o t exec o_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}} the execution feedback. It ends on acceptance or budget exhaustion; its terminal outcome x x earns a reward R ⁡ ( x ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] R(x)\in[0,1] . Problem Statement.
